newsitem.title: USA: U.S. spotlights abuse of children, women.
newsitem.headline: U.S. spotlights abuse of children, women.

text.p: The United States, in its annual human rights report, on Thursday intensified its campaign to focus attention on abuse of children and women.
The State Department report, covering 193 countries, found that 250,000 children, some as young as five, had been conscripted to serve as soldiers in dozens of armed conflicts.

These include armed insurgencies like Cambodia's Khmer Rouge, Peru's Shing Path guerrilla group and some Palestinian groups in Lebanon as well as regular armies in Cambodia, Uganda, Angola and Sudan, the department said.

"Whether it involves ten-year-olds being sent to a battlefield in Liberia or eight-year-olds being sent to work in sweat shops in India, the violation of children's rights is abhorrent and will be a priority for all who care about the development -- their development and about human dignity," Undersecretary of State for Global Affairs Tim Wirth told reporters.
The report said millions of children around the world went uneducated and uncared for and so-called "street children" of major cities were caught in lives of crime and drug dependency.
It also said child prostitution, child pornography and trafficking in children was "all too frequent" in both developed and developing countries.
In India, for instance, there were 500,000 street children, child prostitution was "rampant," and many foetuses found to be female through amniocentisis testing were aborted, it said.
Also, forced prostitution of women was widespread, there were gang rapes as punishment for alleged adultery, and domestic violence over dowry disputes were a serious problem, the report said.

In Pakistan, the use of child and bonded labour remained widespread, little had been done to improve basic conditions for children, and female children had fallen behind their male counterparts in terms of health care and education, the report said.
It was estimated that 80 percent of Pakistani women were victims of domestic violence but police usually returned battered women to their abusive husbands, the report said.

The report found women made some progress in 1996 and it cited development of legislation on family law in Namibia, on violence against women in Ecuador and on women's political participation in the Philippines.
But it said "alongside these gains, however, women all over the world continued to encouter barriers of widespread political, economic and social discrimination, often codified in law."
At a news conference, Wirth stressed that violence against women was "all too prevalent, not only in the developing world but in the most industrialised nations as well."

In a particularly strong indictment, the report concluded that discrimination against women "reached new heights of severity in Afghanistan with the rise to power of the Taliban," the Moslem group that has taken control of most of the country.
"Our focus here is clear: a woman cannot reach her potential and participate in the political life of her country if her basic rights are violated," Wirth said.
